 Description: The defects identified across the metal nuts primarily involve irregularities in color and texture. Common characteristics include:
 - Color Anomalies: Various instances of discoloration manifesting as darker areas, smears, or patches, often contrasting with the surrounding uniform metallic surface. These discolored areas can appear in shades such as blue, red, pink, or indicate variations that differ from the standard metallic gray of the nut.
 - Texture Disruption: Many of the defects are accompanied by scratches or abrasions, typically presenting as linear marks that disrupt the smooth metallic finish. These scratches can be darker than the unaffected areas, suggesting material removal or surface disturbance.
 Overall, these defects indicate potential issues with material inconsistencies, manufacturing processes, or external influences affecting the metal's appearance and integrity, which may compromise the functionality or aesthetic quality of the nuts.
metal_nut.crack:
<crack>
A crack appears as a thin, dark linear discontinuity—often black or deep gray—with irregular, jagged edges and variable length (typically 0.5–3 mm), frequently branching or terminating abruptly; it most commonly occurs on the flat top/bottom surfaces or along the rim of the central hole, and may extend radially from the hole edge or traverse across the nut face; unlike scratches (which are shallow, surface-level and often parallel), cracks exhibit depth-related shadowing, micro-fracture texture, and may interrupt surface patterns or machining marks; they are distinct from chips (which involve material loss with concave voids) and corrosion (which shows diffuse discoloration or pitting).
metal_nut.corrosion:
<corrosion>
Corrosion appears as irregular, reddish-brown to dark orange patches or streaks with a granular, flaky, or powdery texture, often localized on exposed metal surfaces—especially edges, threads, or contact points of the metal nut. It contrasts sharply with the uniform matte gray or silvery finish of healthy stainless or carbon steel, and may exhibit subtle elevation or surface pitting under close inspection. Unlike scratches (which are linear and shallow) or stains (which are smooth and non-textured), corrosion shows progressive color variation, texture coarseness, and tends to spread radially from initiation sites. It is commonly accompanied by loss of metallic luster and may obscure underlying thread geometry.
metal_nut.dent:
<Dent>
A dent appears as a localized, shallow depression or inward deformation on the otherwise smooth, metallic surface of the nut, typically with no material loss or discoloration. It is most commonly found on the flat top or bottom face, or along the side cylindrical surface, often near edges or corners where mechanical impact is likely. The affected region retains the original metallic luster and texture but exhibits subtle shadowing and distorted reflection patterns due to surface curvature change. Unlike scratches (linear, surface-level) or scratches with material removal, dents are broad, rounded, and lack raised edges or color variation.
metal_nut.broken_edge:
<broken_edge>
A broken_edge appears as an irregular, jagged, or missing segment along the otherwise smooth, circular perimeter of the metal nut, often with exposed sharp corners or truncated geometry. It typically occurs at the outer rim or inner thread edge, where mechanical stress or handling damage causes localized material loss. Visually, it contrasts with the uniform metallic sheen and continuous contour of the intact edge, showing either dark shadowed gaps, rough texture, or misaligned geometry. Unlike scratches or dents, broken_edge involves a discontinuity in the edge boundary itself—not surface-level imperfections but actual structural truncation of the part’s silhouette.
metal_nut.threading_error:
<threading_error>
Threading_error appears as distorted, misaligned, or incomplete helical ridges on the threaded portion of the metal nut—often showing flattened, smeared, or asymmetric thread profiles with inconsistent pitch or depth. It occurs exclusively on the internal or external threaded surface, typically spanning multiple adjacent threads rather than isolated spots. Unlike scratches or dents, threading_error exhibits directional periodicity matching the intended thread geometry but with clear geometric deviation (e.g., skewed crest lines, variable groove width, or localized thread merging). It is distinguishable from missing_thread (which shows complete absence of ridges) and burr (which manifests as sharp, extraneous material protrusions at thread edges).
metal_nut.misshapen:
<Misshapen>
A misshapen metal nut exhibits visible geometric distortion in its body or flange—such as asymmetry, uneven curvature, flattened or bulging regions, or non-circular outlines—deviating from the precise cylindrical or toroidal shape expected in a standard nut. It typically occurs across the main body (e.g., distorted hexagonal profile) or flange (e.g., warped, tilted, or elliptical rim), and is distinguishable from scratches or dents by its global form deviation rather than localized surface damage. The defect appears structurally intact (no missing material) but fails dimensional conformity, often with smooth yet incorrect contours and consistent metallic reflectivity. Unlike color anomalies or contamination, misshapen defects retain the base metal’s hue and texture but violate shape priors encoded in CAD models or nominal templates.
metal_nut.missing_part:
<missing_part>
A missing_part defect on a metal_nut appears as an absence of material where a structural feature—such as a threaded section, chamfered edge, or mounting lug—should be present; the region is typically smooth, flat, or irregularly contoured with no texture or geometry matching adjacent functional surfaces. It occurs at predictable locations corresponding to designed features (e.g., missing thread start, absent chamfer on one side, or a missing radial lug), and the boundary between the missing area and intact metal often shows a sharp, clean edge without smearing or deformation. Unlike scratches or dents, it lacks displaced or deformed material; unlike contamination or discoloration, it exhibits no foreign substance or color variation—only geometric incompleteness. It must be distinguished from machining artifacts (e.g., incomplete threading due to tool wear) by verifying whether the missing geometry violates the nominal CAD-defined shape and functional intent.
metal_nut.paint_defect:
<paint_defect>
A paint_defect on a metal_nut appears as an irregular, glossy, often circular or blob-like region with color distinct from the nut’s base metallic finish—typically black, white, or colored paint overspray. It is commonly located on the flat top surface or side rim of the nut, where excess paint has accumulated during coating or handling. Unlike scratches or dents, it exhibits smooth, non-textured, high-contrast reflectivity and lacks depth or material deformation; it can be distinguished from dust or grease spots by its sharper edges and uniform hue.
metal_nut.surface_damage:

Surface damage on metal nuts appears as localized, irregular dark or matte patches—often grayish-black or dull brown—contrasting with the surrounding shiny, metallic surface; it typically occurs on flat top/bottom faces or along the threaded sidewall, manifesting as scratches, scuffs, or shallow abrasions rather than deep gouges or corrosion; unlike corrosion (which shows greenish oxidation or pitting) or contamination (which appears as foreign residue or smudges), surface damage lacks raised texture or color bleeding and preserves the underlying geometry without material loss.

capsule.mold:

hazelnut.scratch:

screw.bend:

This defect is distinguished from normal screw geometry by its non-linear longitudinal axis and from other defects (e.g., thread damage or corrosion) by the absence of localized surface anomalies—only global shape deviation matters. screw.crack:
<Crack>
A crack on a screw appears as a thin, dark linear discontinuity—often black or deep gray—with irregular, jagged edges and variable length (typically 0.1–2 mm wide, up to several millimeters long). It commonly occurs on the screw head (especially near the slot or perimeter), along the shank (parallel to the axis), or at the tip, and may manifest as a surface crack or a through-crack with slight material separation. Unlike scratches (which are shallow, uniform, and often reflective), cracks exhibit depth-related shadowing, lack of continuity in surface texture, and may branch or terminate abruptly—distinguishing them from machining marks, tooling grooves, or oxidation lines.
screw.chip:
<chip>
A chip appears as a small, irregularly shaped missing fragment at the edge or tip of the screw, typically revealing a sharp, angular discontinuity in the otherwise smooth, continuous contour. It is most commonly located at the thread crest, head perimeter, or pointed tip, and exhibits a distinct color/texture contrast—often lighter or more specular due to exposed fresh metal or underlying material. Unlike scratches (linear, surface-level) or dents (depressed, rounded), chips involve actual material loss with visible undercuts or voids, and are distinguishable from normal machining marks by their asymmetry, localized depth, and lack of consistent orientation.
screw.corrosion:
<corrosion>
Corrosion on screws appears as localized brownish-orange or reddish patches, often with a rough, granular, or flaky texture, contrasting sharply with the uniform metallic gray or black finish of healthy screw surfaces. It typically occurs near the head, threads, or tip—especially at edges or crevices where moisture or contaminants accumulate—and may exhibit irregular, spreading boundaries rather than sharp geometric shapes. Unlike scratches (which are linear and glossy) or stains (which are flat and uniform in hue), corrosion shows heterogeneous coloration, micro-pitting, and sometimes slight surface elevation or material loss. It is distinguishable from paint defects by its lack of coating continuity and association with underlying metal degradation.
screw.head_deformity:

A head_deformity appears as an abnormal shape or contour of the screw head, deviating from the intended geometry (e.g., hexagonal, Phillips, flat, or Torx)—common manifestations include flattened, rounded, skewed, asymmetric, or partially missing facets; it is localized exclusively to the topmost surface and perimeter of the screw head, never extending into the shank or thread region; unlike scratches or corrosion, it involves structural distortion rather than surface degradation, and differs from ‘thread_deformity’ by its strict confinement to the head geometry and absence of thread-related irregularities.
screw.tip_defect:
<tip_defect>
A tip_defect appears as a visible deviation from the sharp, conical, and symmetrical geometry expected at the screw’s distal end—commonly manifesting as blunting (flattened or rounded apex), chipping (small missing fragments), cracking (fine linear discontinuities), or complete breakage (abrupt truncation). It is localized exclusively at the very tip of the screw, typically within the top 5–10% of the threaded length, and never extends into the shank or head. Unlike normal manufacturing variations (e.g., minor burrs or slight chamfer inconsistencies), tip_defects exhibit clear loss of structural integrity, asymmetric contours, or non-metallic discoloration (e.g., dark smudges or oxidation at fracture sites). This defect is distinguishable from thread_defects (which affect helical grooves) and head_defects (confined to the upper surface), as it uniquely compromises the functional point of insertion.
screw.dimensional_anomaly:
<Dimensional Anomaly>
A dimensional anomaly on a screw appears as a localized deviation in size—such as an abnormally thick shank, oversized head, elongated thread section, or excessive material buildup—visually disrupting the screw’s expected cylindrical symmetry and smooth profile. It typically occurs along the shank, under the head, or at the tip, and manifests as bulging, tapering irregularities, or non-uniform diameter changes compared to the nominal geometry. Unlike scratches or scratches, it lacks surface texture disruption (e.g., no color change or abrasion marks), and unlike missing parts, it involves excess or misshapen material rather than absence. Its shape is often smoothly contoured but geometrically inconsistent with CAD specifications, detectable via precise edge contour analysis or silhouette mismatch.
screw.dent:

It most commonly occurs on the shank or head of the screw, often aligned with mechanical contact points (e.g., where tools or conveyors pressed against the surface). Unlike scratches or scratches with raised edges, dents lack linear morphology and surface disruption—instead showing subtle shadowing or distorted reflection patterns under directional lighting. They are distinguishable from pits (which involve material removal) and bumps (which protrude outward) by their concave geometry and intact surface finish.

carpet.cut:

carpet.stain:

It typically resides on the surface or slightly penetrates the upper fibers, lacking raised texture or structural deformation. carpet.burn_mark:

A burn mark on carpet appears as a localized, irregularly shaped dark brown or black discolored area, often with charred, melted, or stiffened fibers; it typically occurs on the surface pile and may exhibit slight textural elevation or fiber shrinkage compared to surrounding undamaged carpet. Unlike stains or discolorations, burn marks lack wetness or pigment spread and show sharp, non-diffuse boundaries with possible carbonized residue or fiber denaturation. carpet.fraying:

Fraying appears as loose, tangled, or protruding fibers extending from the carpet surface, often with irregular, wispy, or feathered edges; it typically occurs along cut edges, seams, or high-wear areas such as corners and traffic paths; unlike pilling or fuzzing, fraying involves structural unraveling of the weave or tuft base, showing exposed yarn ends and sometimes underlying backing material; color matches the carpet pile but exhibits heightened texture contrast and directional alignment inconsistent with the surrounding uniform nap.
carpet.wrinkle:
<WRINKLE>

carpet.printing_error:

carpet.pilling:

Small, fuzzy, spherical or irregularly shaped clusters of tangled fibers protruding from the carpet surface, typically light gray to off-white in color and 0.5–3 mm in diameter. carpet.shrinkage:

wood.warp:
<Warp>
A warp defect in wood appears as an abnormal, non-planar deformation—such as bowing, cupping, twisting, or crooking—causing localized surface curvature or misalignment relative to the expected flat or straight geometry. It typically manifests across large contiguous regions (e.g., entire board faces or edges), disrupting uniform grain alignment and creating visible shadow gradients or inconsistent light reflection due to topographic deviation. Unlike cracks or knots, warps lack discontinuities in material continuity; instead, they exhibit smooth, gradual contour changes detectable via shape distortion in overhead imaging or stereo depth cues. Warping is distinguishable from normal wood grain variation by its macro-scale geometric deviation—e.g., a board edge deviating measurably from linearity—or by inconsistent perspective foreshortening in multi-view setups.
wood.water_damage:
<water_damage>
Water damage on wood appears as irregular, darkened, blotchy patches or streaks—often brownish, grayish, or blackish—with a softened, swollen, or slightly raised texture compared to surrounding intact wood. It typically occurs near edges, joints, or low-lying areas where moisture accumulates, and may exhibit subtle warping or grain distortion. Unlike scratches or gouges, it lacks sharp boundaries or material removal; unlike stains from oil or ink, it shows no glossy sheen and often has a matte, damp-looking surface. It is distinguishable from mold by the absence of fuzzy or powdery growth and from natural grain variation by its non-repeating, asymmetric, and moisture-associated morphology.

bottle.contamination:
<Contamination>
 Description: The defects identified present as irregular anomalies within the interior of a bottle's opening. These anomalies generally contrast with the expected uniform dark appearance and smooth texture of the interior surface. Visually, the contamination appears as lighter patches, smudges, cloudy areas, or irregular shapes differing from the surrounding material. Some defects exhibit jagged or rough edges, suggesting foreign substances or residue that compromise the cleanliness and quality of the bottle's contents. The contaminants are typically located at or near the center of the bottle opening, often exhibiting varying colors or textures that disrupt the expected appearance of the product, indicating potential quality control issues in manufacturing or handling.
bottle.broken_large:
<Large Breakage>
 Description: The defect is characterized by significant breakages or chips in the edges of the bottle openings. These defects typically manifest as jagged, irregular breaks with sharp edges that disrupt the otherwise smooth and uniform circular contour of the bottle's rim. The breaks are usually large enough to compromise the structural integrity and functionality of the bottle, often appearing at various positions around the opening, including the center and edges. The exposed surfaces where material is missing contrast starkly with the intact areas of the bottle, showing a deviation in both texture and color. This type of defect presents safety hazards and may lead to product rejection during quality inspections. Useful visual features for distinguishing this defect include the jagged edge appearance, irregular shapes, and the presence of missing or chipped material around the bottle's opening.

The affected area often shows a contrast in texture and color compared to the surrounding surface, with the break appearing lighter or darker than the continuous material. The defect is generally located at various positions around the rim, notably described as being towards the center left, center right, or bottom center, depicting a common vulnerability in the bottle's design.
bottle.circular_discoloration:
<circular_discoloration>
A circular_discoloration appears as a well-defined, roughly circular region on the bottle surface that exhibits a noticeable color and/or brightness difference—either lighter or darker—compared to the surrounding uniform background. It typically occurs on the main cylindrical body or shoulder of the bottle, often with soft or slightly blurred edges, and lacks raised texture or physical deformation. Unlike scratches or dents, it is purely chromatic and photometric, and differs from contamination (e.g., dust or liquid residue) by its symmetric, localized shape and consistent hue shift across the affected area.
bottle.hole:
<Hole>
A hole appears as a circular or near-circular region of missing material, typically revealing the background or underlying surface (e.g., black or dark void if viewed against a light background). It is most commonly located on the bottle’s cylindrical body or shoulder, and ranges from 2–10 mm in diameter—significantly larger than manufacturing micro-voids or surface scratches. Unlike scratches (linear, shallow) or print defects (surface-level color variations), a hole exhibits full-thickness material loss with sharp, well-defined edges and no surrounding discoloration or deformation.
bottle.melted_area:
<Melted_area>
A melted_area appears as a localized, irregularly shaped region on the bottle surface with a glossy, distorted, or warped texture—often darker (brown/black) or discolored (yellowish/amber) compared to the surrounding transparent or colored plastic. It typically occurs near the base, shoulder, or neck of the bottle where thermal stress or overheating during manufacturing (e.g., blow molding or labeling) causes partial melting. Unlike scratches or smudges, it exhibits visible surface deformation (e.g., sagging, bubbling, or loss of contour definition) and lacks sharp edges; it is distinguishable from contamination or stains by its permanent topographic change and absence of particulate or liquid-like reflectance.
bottle.label_defect:
<label_defect>
A label_defect appears as a visibly misaligned, wrinkled, torn, or partially detached label on the bottle’s cylindrical body—often showing uneven edges, gaps between label and surface, or skewed orientation relative to the bottle’s longitudinal axis. It typically occurs on the main labeling area (mid-height of the bottle), and may exhibit color inconsistencies, ink smudging, or text distortion if printed incorrectly. Unlike scratches or dents, it is confined to the label region and retains the label’s base material appearance (e.g., glossy plastic or matte paper), distinguishing it from substrate-level defects like scratches or contamination.
bottle.shape_deformation:
<shape_deformation>
Shape deformation appears as localized or global deviations from the bottle’s intended cylindrical or tapered geometry—such as bulging, denting, twisting, or asymmetric curvature—often visible as irregular contour lines in side-view images. It typically occurs along the body or shoulder region, rarely at the base or neck, and is distinguishable from scratches or stains by its 3D structural nature (e.g., shadow gradients indicating volume change) rather than surface-level texture or color variation. Unlike particle contamination or print defects, shape deformation affects silhouette continuity and disrupts expected edge smoothness and symmetry. It may co-occur with stress marks or micro-cracks but lacks the discrete, high-contrast features of punctures or tears.
bottle.surface_damage:
<surface_damage>
Surface damage on bottles appears as thin, linear, or slightly curved streaks with reduced reflectivity—often appearing as dull, whitish, grayish, or silvery lines against the glossy, transparent or colored bottle surface. It typically occurs on the main cylindrical body or shoulder region, aligned with handling or conveyance direction (e.g., vertical or diagonal), and is distinguishable from dust, stains, or labeling defects by its sharp, elongated morphology and lack of color saturation or particle-like texture. Unlike cracks or dents, surface damage does not disrupt contour continuity or cause light refraction anomalies; unlike bubbles or inclusions, it resides strictly at the outermost surface layer and shows no subsurface depth cues.

 Description: The defect appears as a variety of surface irregularities found on the packaging of numerous food products. The common characteristics of this defect include:
 - Shape: Irregular marks, scratches, dents, or discolorations that disrupt the uniformity and appearance of the box's surface.
 - Color Contrast: Defects often present as darker or lighter areas compared to the surrounding material, indicating a potential smudge, scrape, or indentation. 
 - Texture Difference: The texture can vary from the expected smooth surface; areas affected by the defect may appear dull, scuffed, or otherwise inconsistent with the intact sections of the packaging.
 - Location: Most commonly located towards the center, bottom center, or left areas of the box, affecting logo or graphic designs prominently displayed.
 This surface damage can detract from the product’s aesthetic quality and potentially influence customer perceptions of the product’s integrity or freshness.
food_box.deformation:
<Deformation>
 Description: The defect is characterized by irregularities in the structural integrity of the food packaging boxes, typically manifesting as creased, crushed, or warped areas. The affected sections disrupt the intended flat and smooth surfaces expected from an undamaged box design, leading to distortions in shape, alignment, and visual appeal. The deformation is often located in various regions, including the center, edges, or corners of the boxes. It appears to result from mishandling or pressure during storage or transportation, potentially compromising the aesthetic quality and physical integrity of the product packaging.

 Useful Visual Features for Distinguishing the Defect:
 - Shape Distortion: Look for any bending, warping, or caving-in areas on the box that disrupt straight lines or edges.
 - Texture Changes: Note any visual creases or indentations that deviate from the expected smooth surface.
 - Color Variances: Observe if the affected areas exhibit discoloration or shadows due to light reflection differences, indicating disrupted material integrity.
 - Location Patterns: Commonly found in central sections, edges, or corners of the packaging, indicating specific weaknesses possibly due to compressed packaging.
food_box.opened:

This anomaly reveals that the packaging has been compromised, indicating potential tampering or prior opening. Visual features useful for identifying this defect include irregular shapes, such as an upward protrusion or jagged tear, and discoloration or disturbance in the edges that typically should be sealed flat. Affected areas often appear inconsistent with the normal appearance of the packaging, suggesting that the integrity of the product's contents could be jeopardized, impacting freshness and safety due to possible contamination or environmental exposure. The overall structural uniformity is disturbed, heightening concern for the sealed state expected of new food products.

food_box.Burn Mark:
<Burn Mark>
A Burn Mark appears as a localized, irregularly shaped dark brown or black discoloration on the food_box surface, often with a charred, matte texture and slightly raised or carbonized edges. It typically occurs near heat-exposed areas such as corners, seams, or regions adjacent to sealing equipment, and may exhibit subtle cracking or blistering. Unlike stains or ink smudges, Burn Marks lack glossiness and do not wipe off; they contrast sharply with the box’s base color (e.g., white or light cardboard) and are distinguishable from scratches by their non-linear, thermally diffused boundaries.
food_box.Labeling Issues:
<Missing Label>
A missing label appears as an empty, unprinted rectangular region on the otherwise uniformly colored or textured surface of the food box—typically located on the front or top panel where labeling is expected. It contrasts sharply with surrounding printed areas due to its lack of text, barcode, or graphics, and may show the base substrate (e.g., plain cardboard or white plastic) without ink or adhesive residue. Unlike smudged or faded labels, there is no partial print or ghosting; unlike damaged labels, there are no tears, wrinkles, or peeling edges—only a clean, label-free zone matching the box’s underlying material.
food_box.Missing component:
<Missing component>
A missing component defect appears as an empty, unoccupied region on the food_box where a structural or functional part—such as a lid tab, inner divider, sealing flap, or compartment insert—should be physically present. The defect manifests as a geometrically well-defined void (e.g., rectangular cutout, circular recess, or aligned gap) with clean, sharp edges and background color/texture matching the box’s interior surface, lacking any material, shadow, or contour indicating the expected part. It is typically located at standardized positions: along fold lines, near corners, or centered within compartments—never in arbitrary or irregular locations. This defect is distinguished from scratches or stains by its precise shape and absence of surface disruption, and from misalignment by the complete lack of the component rather than its displaced presence.

cigarette_box.good:
<Normal Characteristics>
 Description: The cigarette boxes displayed in the images exhibit standard characteristics for packaging in this product category. Each box maintains a consistent form and structure, featuring intact edges and corners without any visible tears, dents, or distortions. The color schemes are typically vibrant and aligned with brand specifications, incorporating decorative elements, logos, and text that are clear, sharp, and properly positioned. The design patterns are symmetrical and consistent across the various boxes, with no signs of misprinting or irregular graphics. Minor noise features such as reflections, shadows, and slight variations in color due to lighting conditions are present, but these do not detract from the overall quality and presentation of the boxes. The packaging appears well-preserved, suitable for retail display, and in line with expected standards for cigarette products.
cigarette_box.opened:
<Packaging Tampering>
 Description: The defect involves an alteration in the packaging integrity of cigarette boxes, most notably at the top center where the packaging is supposed to be sealed. Visual cues of this defect include an opened or partially lifted flap, which deviates from the expected flat and flush closure of the box. The affected area often displays signs of discoloration or differences in texture compared to the surrounding packaging, indicating tampering or prior opening. The visual disturbance may manifest as irregular shapes, gaps, or a darker region where the packaging material appears to have been disturbed. Such anomalies compromise the integrity and cleanliness of the product, raising concerns for quality control and consumer trust.
cigarette_box.surface_damage:
<surface_damage>
Surface damage on cigarette boxes manifests as localized deformations (dents, creases, or crushed areas), linear disruptions (scratches, tears, or cracks), or material failures (peeling cellophane, torn corners, or lifted labels), typically appearing as irregular contours, discontinuous edges, or altered reflectivity compared to the smooth, uniform glossy surface of intact packaging. It commonly occurs on flat panel surfaces, corners, lid edges, or seam lines—especially where mechanical impact or compression is likely during handling or shipping. Unlike printing defects (e.g., smudged logos) or contamination (e.g., stains), surface damage involves physical topography changes: dents show shadowed concavities, scratches appear as fine, linear, matte streaks, and tears reveal underlying layers or substrate texture. It must be distinguished from intentional design features (e.g., embossed branding) by its asymmetry, sharp boundaries, and contextual inconsistency with adjacent undamaged regions.
cigarette_box.color_inconsistency:
<color_inconsistency>
Color inconsistency appears as localized areas on the cigarette box surface where the printed colors deviate noticeably from the expected hue, saturation, or brightness—often manifesting as faded, washed-out, yellowed, or unevenly toned regions. It commonly occurs on high-contrast graphic elements (e.g., logos, brand text, or background panels) and is frequently observed near the top edge, corners, or along fold lines where ink adhesion or exposure may be compromised. Unlike stains or physical damage, it lacks texture change or surface deformation; unlike printing misalignment, it affects color fidelity without shifting pattern geometry. It must be distinguished from normal gloss variation or lighting-induced specular highlights by verifying consistent chromatic deviation across multiple viewing angles and illumination conditions.
cigarette_box.branding_damage:
<branding_damage>
Branding damage appears as localized disruptions—such as scratches, scuffs, tears, smudges, or fading—in the printed graphics, logos, or decorative ribbon on the cigarette box surface; it typically occurs on the front or top panel where branding elements are prominently placed; unlike structural defects (e.g., dents or creases), branding damage affects only the visual layer without altering the box’s geometry or material integrity, and it is distinguishable from color variation or printing misalignment by its irregular, non-uniform, and physically degraded texture.
cigarette_box.closure_issue:
<closure_issue>
A closure_issue on a cigarette_box appears as a visible misalignment, gap, or separation between the top flap and the main body—often with uneven edges, wrinkled paper, or partial lifting of the adhesive seal. It typically occurs at the upper front edge where the lid meets the box, and may show white paper substrate exposure, creasing, or asymmetrical overlap compared to the intact side. This defect is distinguished from normal wear by its sharp, localized discontinuity (not gradual fading) and absence of intentional design features like perforations or embossing. Unlike tearing or puncture defects, closure_issue lacks fiber rupture or jagged material loss—it is primarily a geometric or adhesive failure.
cigarette_box.packaging_anomaly:
<packaging_anomaly>
A packaging_anomaly on a cigarette_box appears as irregular deformations, wrinkles, tears, or misaligned flaps in the outer cardboard or foil wrapping—often with unnatural creasing, glossy or matte surface inconsistencies, or localized buckling. It typically occurs at seam lines, corners, or flap closures where folding or sealing should be precise and flush. Unlike normal printing variations or minor scuffs, this defect exhibits structural deviation (e.g., lifted edges, overlapping layers, or protruding material) that compromises package integrity and visual uniformity.
cigarette_box.labeling_defect:
<labeling_defect>
A labeling_defect on a cigarette_box appears as either a completely missing label, a visibly misaligned (crooked, skewed, or shifted) label, or a label with incorrect text/logo/branding. It typically occurs on the front, top, or side panels where branding and regulatory information must be precisely positioned. The defect is distinguished from normal regions by abrupt absence of expected printed content, irregular label edges, inconsistent spacing relative to panel borders, or mismatched typography/colors compared to the ground-truth label design. Unlike printing defects (e.g., smudging or fading), labeling_defects involve structural or positional errors—such as label absence, rotation >5°, lateral offset >2 mm, or substitution with wrong variant—rather than degradation of an otherwise correctly placed label.
cigarette_box.edge_irregularity:
<edge_irregularity>
Edge irregularity appears as a non-uniform, wavy, jagged, or buckled contour along the normally sharp, straight edges of the cigarette box—most commonly at the top center or side seams—where the cardboard fails to fold or seal cleanly. It manifests as localized protrusions, inward dents, or inconsistent edge alignment, often accompanied by visible creasing, overlapping flaps, or slight warping of the laminated surface. Unlike normal minor printing misalignments or surface scratches, edge irregularity affects the structural geometry and silhouette of the box, disrupting the expected crisp rectangular outline in top-down or frontal views. It is distinguishable from corner damage (which involves chipping or tearing) and from label misalignment (which only affects printed graphics, not the physical edge shape).
cigarette_box.missing_component:
<missing_component>
A missing_component defect appears as an empty, unoccupied region on the cigarette box where a required element—such as a foil seal, inner lid, printed logo, or embossed feature—should be visibly present. It is typically located in standardized positions: center-top of the lid (for foil seals), inner flap surface (for lining or branding), or front panel (for logos or regulatory text). The defect region often exhibits uniform background color/texture matching the underlying substrate (e.g., plain cardboard or foil base) with sharp, geometric boundaries contrasting against adjacent printed or textured areas—distinguishing it from smudges, scratches, or misprints.

food_bottle.good:
<Normal Characteristics>
 Description: The food containers depicted in the images exhibit typical characteristics expected of commercially packaged food products. The shapes of the containers are round or cylindrical, with intact and properly seated lids or seals. The labels are clear and well-aligned, presenting vibrant colors and graphics that are free from tears, misprints, or misalignments. There are no visible dents, scratches, distortions, or damages that would indicate flaws in the integrity of the containers. The background elements, such as reflections and shadows from the lighting conditions, are typical in product photography and are not considered defects. The overall appearance of these food containers indicates they are ready for retail, maintaining the expected standards for packaging in terms of presentation and usability. The consistency in design and manufacturing across all product types suggests they meet the quality expectations set for such items in the market.
food_bottle.surface_damage:
<Surface Damage>
 Description: The defect present is characterized by irregularities on the surface of various cylindrical food containers. These anomalies can manifest as discoloration, dents, scratches, or distortions that interrupt the otherwise smooth and consistent appearance of the product's packaging. The impacted areas often exhibit a noticeable difference in color or texture compared to the surrounding surface, suggesting potential flaws related to manufacturing, handling, or transportation. Such surface damage can affect the visual appeal and perceived quality of the product, raising concerns regarding its integrity and shelf life.
food_bottle.deformation:
<Deformation>
 Description: The defect observed across the various food containers is consistently categorized as deformation. This manifests as an irregularity in the shape of the containers, often appearing as indents, warps, or crushed areas, primarily concentrated around the central or upper regions of the packaging. The deformations disrupt the normal cylindrical or rounded appearance of the containers, undermining their structural integrity. Visually, these defects could present as inward dents, caved-in sections, crumpled edges, or bulging areas, suggesting that the containers may have been subjected to undue force or pressure during production, transportation, or handling. This type of defect can potentially compromise the seal of the containers, affecting the freshness and safety of the enclosed products.
food_bottle.opened:
<Compromised Seal/Opened Packaging>
 Description: The defect appears as an opening, tear, or irregularity at the top center of cylindrical food containers, indicating that the seal has been broken or is not properly secured. This defect can manifest as areas where the lid is peeling back, exposing the interior, or where the supplied seal is disrupted, resulting in a visible change in color or texture. Such anomalies compromise the integrity and safety of the contents inside, potentially leading to spoilage, contamination, or loss of product freshness. Regular characteristics of a properly sealed container include a smooth and intact lid that fits flush against the rim, indicating the product is untampered and suitable for consumption. The presence of defects in the opening mechanism is critical, especially for food products, as it raises concerns regarding hygiene and quality control.
food_bottle.contamination:
<contamination>
Contamination appears as abnormal discoloration (e.g., brown, green, or cloudy patches) or foreign particulates suspended in the liquid contents of the bottle; it is typically localized within the transparent or semi-transparent body of the food bottle, visible through the container wall or cap seal area. Unlike normal sediment or labeling artifacts, contamination exhibits irregular shape, non-uniform texture, and color inconsistent with the expected product hue (e.g., milky opacity in clear juice or dark specks in light-colored sauce). It is distinct from surface-level label smudges or condensation because it resides inside the sealed bottle and does not shift with bottle orientation.
food_bottle.Incorrect label:
<Incorrect label>
An incorrect label appears as a visibly mismatched, misaligned, peeling, discolored, scratched, or partially missing adhesive label on the food bottle surface; it commonly occurs on the front or side body of the bottle where branding and product information are printed, and may show inconsistent colors, blurred/misprinted text, exposed substrate, or glossy/shiny spots contrasting with the surrounding matte label area; unlike normal labels, it exhibits irregular edges, lifting corners, ink smudging, or complete absence of expected graphics/logos, and must be distinguished from benign surface scratches (which affect the bottle itself, not the label layer) or dust (which lacks sharp geometric boundaries and label-specific typography).
food_bottle.Missing lid:
<Missing lid>
A missing lid appears as an open, circular aperture at the top of the food bottle, where the expected opaque, flat or slightly domed cap (typically metallic silver, white, or colored plastic) is entirely absent. The exposed opening reveals the inner neck threads and sometimes the product surface or seal liner, creating a stark contrast in texture and reflectivity compared to the intact, sealed bottle body. It is always located at the very top center of the bottle, aligned with the longitudinal axis, and must be distinguished from partial lid misalignment, loose lids, or intact but discolored lids — all of which retain physical coverage of the opening.
food_bottle.Leakage:
<Leakage>
Leakage appears as wet, shiny, or discolored patches—often brownish, yellowish, or translucent—on the bottle surface, especially near seals, caps, or seams; it may be accompanied by dried residue trails or sticky film. It typically occurs at the cap-thread interface, base seal, or side seam where structural integrity is compromised. Unlike condensation (which is uniform and evaporates quickly), leakage leaves persistent stains, has irregular edges, and may show signs of product seepage (e.g., syrupy texture or odor residue). It is distinguishable from scratches or labeling defects by its fluid-related visual cues and localized moisture evidence.
food_bottle.seal_defect:
<seal_defect>
A seal_defect appears as a visible discontinuity at the bottle’s cap-to-body interface—typically appearing as peeling, lifting, tearing, or partial detachment of the inner foil or plastic seal. It is located exclusively at the top rim of the bottle, directly beneath the screw cap, and often shows exposed adhesive residue, wrinkled or curled seal edges, or gaps between the seal and container surface. Unlike normal shrink bands (which are intact, uniformly tight, and circumferential), this defect exhibits asymmetric deformation, localized separation, or foreign material intrusion (e.g., fingerprints or debris) at the seal boundary. It must be distinguished from cap misalignment or labeling defects by confirming the absence of intact, continuous seal material bridging the cap–bottle junction.

 Description: The defect is characterized by visible irregularities on the surface of various packaged food products. These anomalies appear as darkened areas, discolorations, or smudges that contrast with the surrounding packaging material, disrupting the visual continuity and aesthetic appeal. The affected areas often lack a defined shape and may suggest underlying issues such as scratches, dents, or printing errors that affect the uniform appearance of the package. As a result, these surface anomalies could potentially raise concerns regarding the product's integrity, quality, and safety, impacting consumer perceptions and marketability.
food_package.broken:
<Packaging Compromise>
 Description: The defect is characterized by various forms of damage to the packaging of food products, primarily observed as tears or ruptures that disrupt the integrity of the seal. Common visual features include irregular edges and regions that exhibit discoloration or changes in texture compared to the surrounding areas. The anomalies are often located at the top center or upper corners of the package, making them prominent against the overall design. The compromised areas typically suggest exposure to external elements, which could lead to spoilage or contamination of the product inside. Markers indicative of breaks or punctures are present, often highlighted by altered reflectivity or a loss of uniformity in the packaging material. This type of defect is critical to identify as it affects the product's freshness and safety, necessitating removal from distribution to maintain quality standards.
food_package.good:
<Normal Characteristics>
 Description: The food packages appear intact with no visible defects or anomalies. They maintain a proper shape, are upright, and are well-sealed, suggesting they are suitable for retail display. The printing on each package is clear, including branding, product information, and any imagery, with no smudges, misalignments, or misprints. The color schemes of the packages are vibrant and consistent, aligned with their intended designs. Minor reflections, shadows, and light noise present in the images are typical of packaging materials and environments, and they do not indicate defects. Any slight creases or irregularities seen are standard characteristics of flexible packaging and do not compromise the integrity of the packages. Overall, the products represent a standard, undamaged condition expected for food items prepared for retail sale.
food_package.compromised_integrity:
<compromised_integrity>
Compromised integrity appears as visible tears, punctures, splits, or severe creasing in the food package material—often revealing underlying layers or exposing contents; it typically occurs along seams, corners, or stress points (e.g., bottom folds or seal edges) and may show jagged edges, localized thinning, or irregular deformations. Unlike normal wrinkles or minor scuffing, this defect exhibits structural failure—such as open gaps, displaced laminate layers, or light transmission through damaged areas—and is distinguishable from discoloration or printing defects by its physical discontinuity and loss of containment function.
food_package.contamination:
<contamination>
Contamination appears as foreign material—such as dust, hair, insect parts, or debris—on the surface of the food package, often contrasting sharply in color (e.g., dark specks on light packaging or vice versa) and texture (gritty, fibrous, or irregularly shaped). It typically occurs on flat, visible areas like the front panel, seal region, or transparent window of the package, and may be partially embedded or loosely adhering. Unlike printing defects or scratches, contamination lacks geometric regularity and does not follow package contours; it is distinguishable from normal packaging textures by its isolated, non-uniform morphology and inconsistent reflectivity under standard lighting.
food_package.discoloration:
<Discoloration>
Discoloration appears as localized areas where the printed graphics or packaging surface deviate in hue, saturation, or brightness from the surrounding normal region—commonly manifesting as faded, duller, darker, or blotchy patches. It typically occurs on flat, printed regions of the food package (e.g., front panel, label area) and lacks raised texture or physical deformation, distinguishing it from scratches, dents, or contamination. Unlike stains or foreign residue, discoloration shows no evidence of surface wetness, particulates, or layer delamination, and unlike printing misregistration, the graphic layout remains geometrically intact—only color fidelity is compromised. The affected zone often has soft, ill-defined edges and may exhibit subtle gradients rather than sharp boundaries.
food_package.deformation:
<Deformation>
A deformation appears as an unnatural, localized physical distortion of the food package surface—such as dents, creases, crumples, or compressions—that disrupts the expected smooth, rigid, or uniformly contoured geometry. It typically occurs on flat or curved panel areas (e.g., front/back labels, side walls, or top seals) and manifests as irregular indentations, sharp folds, or flattened zones with altered reflectivity or shadowing compared to surrounding intact material. Unlike tears or punctures, deformations retain material continuity (no breaks or holes), and unlike printing defects, they involve 3D shape deviation visible under varied lighting angles. Crumpling often shows chaotic, multi-directional wrinkles, while dents are more localized, radially compressed depressions—both contrasting sharply with the taut, planar, or smoothly curved baseline geometry of undamaged packaging.
food_package.incorrect_labeling:
<incorrect_labeling>
Incorrect labeling appears as a complete absence of the label, partial peeling or lifting (often with visible curling edges and adhesive exposure), misaligned placement (e.g., skewed, off-center, or rotated), or printing errors such as smudged, faded, blurred, or missing text/graphics. It occurs exclusively on the primary label area—typically the front or top panel of the food package—and is distinguishable from normal packaging by the lack of expected branding elements, inconsistent typography, or physical discontinuity (e.g., air bubbles, wrinkles, or torn edges) not present in correctly applied labels.
food_package.foreign_object:
<foreign_object>
Foreign objects appear as anomalous, non-packaging elements inside or on the food package—commonly including metal shards, plastic fragments, hair, insects, or debris—often contrasting sharply in color (e.g., dark hair on light-colored snacks, metallic glint on glossy film) and texture (e.g., irregular edges, specular highlights, or matte opacity inconsistent with the packaging material). They are typically located within the sealed product area (visible through transparent packaging) or embedded in seal regions, and may partially occlude underlying content. Unlike printing defects or scratches, foreign objects exhibit independent shape, scale, and material properties inconsistent with the package’s design, substrate, or expected food contents—and are never part of the intended structural or graphic elements.
food_package.straight_line_defect:
<Straight_line_defect>
A straight_line_defect appears as a thin, continuous, high-contrast linear feature—typically black or dark gray—running across the food_package surface, often orthogonal or parallel to package edges. It commonly occurs on printed label areas or laminated film surfaces, where it may result from ink smearing, scratch marks, or misaligned printing rollers. Unlike natural creases or folds, this defect exhibits uniform width, sharp edges, and geometric rigidity without curvature or branching. It is distinguishable from wrinkles (which are wavy and irregular) and dust streaks (which are fainter and less consistent in contrast and continuity).

drink_bottle.good:

Any reflections, shadows, or variations in the background observed in the images are attributed to environmental conditions and lighting rather than defects in the products themselves. These noise features are typical in retail environments, ensuring that the bottles maintain a standard appearance characteristic of undamaged, retail-ready beverage packaging.
drink_bottle.surface_damage:

 Description: The defect manifests as irregularities or imperfections on the surface of plastic or glass bottles, often impacting the labels or overall exterior condition. Common characteristics include discoloration, distortion, scratches, dents, or smudged areas that disrupt the visual continuity of the product design. These anomalies typically indicate potential issues with the product's packaging integrity and aesthetics, which may affect consumer perception and quality control standards. The defects consistently occur at various positions on the bottles, with notable locations including the center, bottom center, or label areas, and they may result from handling, manufacturing defects, or environmental exposure during storage or transport.
drink_bottle.cap_open:
<Open Cap>
 Description: The defect involves the cap of the beverage bottle not being fully sealed or slightly ajar, as expected in a properly packaged product. This defect is typically located at the top center of the bottle, where the cap meets the neck. The appearance of the defect usually indicates a gap between the cap and the bottle, suggesting potential tampering or a failure in the sealing process during manufacturing. A properly sealed cap should fit snugly against the bottle neck, ensuring product integrity and safety. This defect can compromise freshness, lead to contamination, and affect the overall quality and shelf life of the beverage inside.
drink_bottle.cap_half_open:

This defect is critical as it compromises the seal integrity of the product, potentially leading to contamination or degradation of the beverage inside, thereby affecting its freshness and safety for consumption. Such defects can manifest as subtle shifts in alignment or gaps that deviate from the expected fully sealed position of the cap, posing significant risks for both product integrity and consumer trust.
drink_bottle.Absence of label or branding:
<Absence of label or branding>
A missing label or branding appears as a smooth, unprinted, uniform surface—typically matching the base bottle material (e.g., translucent PET, opaque white plastic, or colored resin)—where a label or printed logo should be located. It is most commonly observed on the central frontal or lateral body region of the bottle, often bounded by adjacent printed elements or label edges; unlike scratches or smudges, it lacks texture variation, color gradients, or ink residue. This defect is distinguished from label misalignment (which shows partial or skewed label presence) and label damage (which retains visible fragments, creases, or discoloration), as it exhibits complete absence of any printed or adhesive label content in the expected region.
drink_bottle.contamination:
<contamination>
Contamination on drink bottles appears as irregular, non-uniform patches or droplets of foreign material—often darker (brown, yellow, or green) or translucent—on the bottle surface, typically near the base, cap thread, or label area. It may have a glossy, sticky, or granular texture distinct from the smooth, uniform finish of clean PET or glass. Unlike scratches or dents, contamination lacks sharp edges and does not deform the bottle geometry; it is often localized and may exhibit smearing or pooling behavior. It must be distinguished from label glue residue (which is usually confined to label edges) and condensation (which evaporates quickly and lacks coloration or adhesion).
drink_bottle.label_damage:
<label_damage>
Label damage appears as localized discoloration (e.g., yellowing, browning, or faded patches), creases, wrinkles, indentations, or partial tearing on the otherwise smooth, uniformly printed label surface. It typically occurs on the main body or shoulder region of the drink bottle where the label is applied, and may distort text, logos, or background graphics—breaking visual continuity without affecting the bottle’s structural integrity. Unlike normal label curvature or printing variations, label damage exhibits abrupt texture changes (e.g., raised or compressed areas) or color anomalies inconsistent with adjacent label regions. It is distinguishable from contamination (e.g., smudges or liquid residue) by its fixed, non-removable appearance and alignment with physical deformation or aging-related degradation of the label material.
drink_bottle.discoloration:
<Discoloration>
Discoloration on drink bottles appears as a localized or widespread area that is noticeably darker, lighter, or differently shaded compared to the surrounding surface—often lacking texture change but exhibiting uniform color deviation (e.g., yellowing, browning, or graying). It commonly occurs on the bottle body, shoulder, or label region, and may cover smooth curved surfaces without disrupting gloss or contour. Unlike scratches or dents, discoloration lacks topographic variation and does not reflect light differently; unlike stains, it typically has soft, diffuse boundaries rather than sharp, irregular edges. It must be distinguished from intentional design elements (e.g., gradient labels) by its unintended, non-symmetrical, and inconsistent appearance relative to the product’s reference color map.
drink_bottle.barcode_damage:
<barcode_damage>
A barcode_damage appears as localized visual corruption within the printed barcode region—typically manifesting as smudging, blurring, scratches, ink fading, or partial erasure of the black-and-white parallel bars. It is strictly confined to the rectangular barcode area, usually located on the lower rear or side label of the drink_bottle, and never extends into adjacent label text or background graphics. Unlike label_scratch (which affects broader label areas) or print_smudge (which may appear anywhere on printed surfaces), barcode_damage preserves the barcode’s overall rectangular outline but disrupts the high-contrast, evenly spaced bar pattern required for scanning. The defect reduces barcode legibility by breaking bar continuity, introducing false gaps, or merging adjacent bars—often resulting in low-intensity or noisy pixel regions where sharp binary transitions should exist.
drink_bottle.neck_damage:
<neck_damage>
A neck_damage appears as a visible deformation, crack, or break in the narrow cylindrical section connecting the bottle body to the cap—typically near the top rim. It may manifest as jagged fractures, flattened or bent contours, chipped edges, or localized discoloration (e.g., white stress lines or dark fracture shadows), contrasting with the smooth, uniform texture and consistent curvature of the intact neck. This defect is strictly confined to the neck region—never extending into the shoulder or cap—and must be distinguished from benign labeling artifacts, condensation, or reflections by its structural discontinuity and geometric distortion.
drink_bottle.label_defect:
<label_defect>
A label_defect on a drink_bottle appears as a visible anomaly in the printed or applied label—such as misalignment, creasing, bubbling, tearing, smudging, fading, or partial/complete absence of the label—typically located on the cylindrical body or shoulder region of the bottle. It contrasts with the intended smooth, uniform, and fully adhered label surface, often showing irregular edges, color inconsistencies, or texture discontinuities (e.g., wrinkles or air pockets). Unlike cap defects or base scratches, label_defects are confined to the labeled area and do not affect structural integrity but compromise branding clarity and aesthetic consistency.
drink_bottle.leakage:
<leakage>
Leakage appears as wet, shiny, or discolored patches—often darker or stained—on the bottle’s bottom, cap seal, or seam junctions, caused by liquid seeping out. It may be accompanied by visible droplets, residue trails, or crystallized deposits (e.g., sugar rings) around the leak site. Unlike normal condensation (which is uniform and evaporates quickly), leakage persists, spreads along gravity-dependent paths, and often disrupts surface texture with smearing or stickiness. It is distinct from scratches or labeling defects because it involves material evidence of liquid escape—typically localized to sealing interfaces rather than random surface areas.
drink_bottle.label_peeling:
<label_peeling>
Label peeling appears as a partially detached, lifted, or curled edge of the printed label—often with visible white adhesive backing or underlying bottle surface exposed. It typically occurs along the top, bottom, or side seams of the label, especially near corners or edges where adhesion is weakest. The peeled region contrasts sharply with the intact label in texture (wrinkled or buckled vs. smooth), color (exposed clear plastic or white adhesive vs. printed label), and contour (raised or folded geometry). Unlike label fading or printing defects, peeling involves physical separation from the bottle surface and may show light reflection differences or shadowing at the lift point.
drink_bottle.rough_texture:
<rough_texture>
A rough texture appears as a localized region on the bottle surface with visibly irregular, grainy, or sandpaper-like topography—often lacking the smooth, glossy finish of normal PET or glass bottle surfaces. It typically occurs on the main body or shoulder area, and may exhibit subtle matte contrast or light-scattering under uniform illumination. Unlike scratches (linear, directional) or contamination (foreign particles), rough texture shows diffuse, non-directional micro-irregularities without sharp edges or discrete foreign material. It is distinguishable from normal label textures or mold seams by its unstructured, non-repeating, and abnormally tactile-like visual signature in high-resolution images.
drink_bottle.shiny_spot:
<shiny_spot>
A shiny spot appears as an abnormally bright, highly reflective circular or oval region on the bottle surface, often with a mirror-like sheen that contrasts sharply with the surrounding matte or semi-gloss finish. It typically occurs on the main body or shoulder of the drink bottle, where uneven coating, polishing residue, or localized surface contamination (e.g., oil or silicone) creates anomalous light reflection. Unlike normal label gloss or intentional embossed highlights, a shiny spot lacks defined edges, shows no underlying texture or print, and exhibits specular reflection that shifts dramatically with viewing angle. It is distinguishable from scratches (which are linear and scattering) and stains (which are diffuse and often discolored) by its uniform brightness, lack of color shift, and absence of physical deformation.
drink_bottle.transparency_defect:
<transparency_defect>
A transparency_defect appears as an abnormally clear, glossy, or glass-like region on the otherwise matte or semi-opaque surface of a drink bottle—often lacking the expected label texture, color saturation, or surface diffusion. It typically occurs on the bottle’s main body or shoulder area where printed labels or molded textures should be present, manifesting as a localized spot or irregular patch that reflects light more intensely and appears visually “thinner” or “see-through” compared to surrounding material. Unlike scratches or smudges, it lacks raised/lowered topography or contaminant residue; unlike color fading, it shows no gradual hue shift but rather a sudden loss of opacity and visual depth. It may be accompanied by subtle refractive distortion when viewed at an angle, distinguishing it from simple gloss variation or lighting glare.
drink_bottle.structural_weakness:
<structural_weakness>
A structural weakness appears as an abnormal thinning, localized deformation, or subtle crease in the bottle wall—often with no discoloration but visible as a slight inward bowing, waviness, or asymmetry under uniform lighting. It typically occurs along the cylindrical body or shoulder region, where mechanical stress concentrates, and is distinguishable from normal mold seams by its irregular contour and lack of consistent linear pattern. Unlike cracks or fractures, it shows no discontinuity in surface continuity or light reflection, and differs from dents by lacking sharp edges or abrupt depth change.

drink_can.straw_missing:
<Missing Straw>
 Description: The defect is characterized by the absence of a straw that is typically affixed to the beverage carton. This missing component is commonly located around the center of the packaging, where it is usually attached with clear adhesive. The defect is easily distinguishable by examining the area that is expected to hold the straw, which appears empty or smooth compared to a normal sample where the straw is present. Its absence affects the functionality of the product, as the straw is crucial for convenient consumption of the beverage. Overall, the defect signifies a packaging flaw that deviates from expected product standards, potentially impacting user experience.
drink_can.good:
<Normal Characteristics>
 Description: The inspected beverage can and carton packaging objects show a consistent pattern of characteristics typical for commercial packaging. They are intact without any visible defects such as dents, tears, or printing errors. The labels are well-applied, vibrant in color, and free from misprints, smudging, or inconsistencies. The physical integrity of each package is maintained, with no evident deformations or damage. Accessories such as straws, which may be attached to certain cartons, are correctly affixed and serve their intended purpose for easy consumption. The background features, including patterns and reflections, are recognized as normal environmental noise during photography and do not implicate any anomalies in the presented products. Overall, all items conform to the expected visual and structural standards for their respective food and beverage packaging.
drink_can.surface_damage:
<Surface Damage>
 Description: The defect manifests as various forms of surface damage, characterized primarily by irregularities that disrupt the continuity of the can's surface. These irregularities may include scratches, dents, or discolorations that contrast with the surrounding area. The affected regions often exhibit changes in sheen, texture, or color, indicating potential compromise to the aesthetic and possibly structural integrity of the can. Such defects are typically observed around the center, top, or bottom sections of the can and may vary in severity from minor blemishes to more significant deformities that reveal the underlying material or coating. The nature of these imperfections detracts from the visual appeal of the product and may raise concerns about handling, storage, or manufacturing quality.
drink_can.deformation:
<Carton Deformation>
 Description: The defect observed across the batch of beverage cartons is characterized as a deformation. This manifests as irregular indentations, crumpled areas, or compressions, predominantly affecting the structural integrity of the cartons. The distortions typically occur near the center, sides, or top of the carton, leading to irregular shapes that deviate from the expected smooth, rectangular form. The affected areas may disrupt the continuity of printed graphics and text, suggesting potential issues with product sealing and freshness. The defects could indicate mishandling or abnormal pressure applied during storage or transportation, which compromises the overall aesthetic and functionality of the packaging.
drink_can.color_fade:
<color_fade>
Color_fade appears as a localized or widespread reduction in pigment intensity on the can’s printed label or metallic surface, often manifesting as pale, washed-out, or yellowish/brownish patches compared to the vibrant, uniform baseline color. It typically occurs on the main body of the can—especially areas exposed to UV light, heat, or abrasion—and may follow a gradient or irregular boundary rather than sharp edges. Unlike scratches or dents, it lacks topographic change and retains smooth surface texture; unlike ink smudging or printing defects, it shows no ink bleeding, blurring, or misregistration. It is distinguishable from rust (which exhibits reddish-brown flaking) and corrosion (which shows pitting or white residue) by its uniform matte appearance and absence of material degradation.
drink_can.label_defect:
<label_defect>
A label_defect on a drink_can appears as a misaligned, wrinkled, torn, or partially detached paper or plastic label—often with visible gaps, creases, skewed orientation, or inconsistent spacing relative to the can’s top/bottom edges. It typically occurs on the cylindrical body of the can, where the label should be centered and flush; defects may also include wrong label content (e.g., mismatched brand or flavor) or complete absence of label in the expected region. Unlike normal wear (e.g., light scuffing), label_defects show abrupt geometric discontinuities—such as sharp folds, white exposed substrate, or asymmetric margins—and are distinguishable from print defects (which affect ink only) by involving physical label integrity and placement.
drink_can.crack:
<crack>
A crack appears as a thin, linear, dark fissure—often black or deep gray—with irregular edges and slight texture discontinuity; it typically occurs on the curved aluminum body of the drink can, especially near seams, dents, or stress points. Unlike scratches (which are superficial and follow surface grain) or scratches with metal exposure (which show bright metallic sheen), cracks reveal underlying material separation and may exhibit micro-fracture branching or localized deformation. It is distinguishable from creases (which are folded metal with uniform shadowing) and dents (which are broad depressions without linear discontinuity).
drink_can.hole:
<hole>
A hole appears as a small, circular or irregularly shaped opening penetrating through the metal surface of the drink can, typically revealing the underlying background or interior space. It is most commonly located on the cylindrical body or lid, and visually manifests as a dark, void-like region with sharp or slightly deformed edges, often surrounded by minor burrs or discoloration from material deformation. Unlike scratches or dents, a hole exhibits complete material loss and optical transparency (or background visibility) at the defect site, distinguishing it from surface-level imperfections.
drink_can.tear:
<Tear>
A tear on a drink_can appears as an irregular, jagged linear discontinuity in the metal or printed label surface, often with raised or curled edges and exposed underlying material (e.g., bare aluminum or adhesive layer). It typically occurs along the can body—especially near the top rim, seam, or label edges—and may range from 1–10 mm in length, with visible distortion of adjacent print or texture. Unlike scratches (which are shallow and surface-level) or dents (which involve inward deformation), a tear exhibits physical separation of material layers and may show light reflection differences due to edge elevation and micro-shadowing.
